findings.headline: Settlement funding sensitivity creates £35M variance in three-year budget gap between optimistic and pessimistic scenarios.
findings.detail: The council's budget is highly sensitive to Welsh Government settlement levels, with each 1% change impacting the budget gap by £5.6M annually. Modelling ranges from +3% growth (three-year gap of £55.4M) to +1% growth (three-year gap of £90.1M), a swing of £34.7M. This means the final funding requirement is substantially determined by political funding decisions outside the council's control.
findings.matters: High sensitivity to external funding creates forecast uncertainty; councils dependent on volatile funding streams face difficulty planning, and lenders have reduced visibility of actual outturn until settlements are confirmed.
findings.figures: Sensitivity analysis shows £5.6M impact per 1% change in settlement (section 6.1); Figure 1 base-case scenarios show 3-year gap of £55,409k (at +3% WG resource) vs £90,144k (at +1% WG resource)
findings.quote: The variability of the potential level of the Settlement from Welsh Government has a significant impact on the budget gap, at £5.6M per 1%

findings.headline: Council anticipates significant service reductions and workforce changes to close the budget gap.
findings.detail: The council states it is "highly likely that revisions to some service delivery arrangements will be required and associated staffing levels." While services will be protected "wherever possible," the scale of the gap requires changes to delivery models and staffing. Service-level reductions are listed as "a last resort" but are acknowledged as likely given the sustained significant budget gaps.
findings.matters: Service reductions and workforce cuts signal deteriorating service capacity; councils making large cuts face operational risk and may struggle to meet statutory obligations in areas like social care, affecting their creditworthiness.
findings.figures: £36.9M Additional Budget Requirement in 2027/28 alone; three-year cumulative additional requirement £107.0M (Figure 1)
findings.quote: it is highly likely that revisions to some service delivery arrangements will be required and associated staffing levels, based on the continued significant budget gaps which we face

findings.headline: Reserves inadequate to bridge structural deficit; £150M+ depletion still leaves £73M of permanent budget cuts needed.
findings.detail: The council's Medium-Term Financial Plan shows that using reserves alone to balance the budget would require over £150M of draw-downs over the three-year period, yet the council would still require approximately £73M of permanent base-budget reductions by the end of the planning period. This demonstrates reserves cannot sustainably address the structural deficit.
findings.matters: Reserves depletion signals weakening financial resilience; simultaneous reserve exhaustion and base-budget cuts indicate the council has limited tools left to manage the deficit, creating acute liquidity pressure.
findings.figures: £150M+ reserves required; £73M permanent base-budget cuts still needed despite reserve depletion (section 8.3); base-case 3-year budget gap £72,947k (Figure 1)
findings.quote: to balance the budget (base case) using reserves alone would require the use of over £150M of reserves and the Council would still have a need to reduce its base budget by approximately £73M at the end of this period

findings.headline: Council faces £25.7M budget gap in 2027/28 in a multi-year structural deficit.
findings.detail: The council is modelling a base-case budget gap of £25.7M for 2027/28 (before Council Tax increases), followed by gaps of £25.6M and £21.7M in subsequent years, totalling £72.9M over three years at 2% Welsh Government settlement growth. This follows a pattern of gaps exceeding £20M in the current year and £30M+ in each of the three years prior.
findings.matters: A council with consistent multi-year deficits of this scale faces ongoing risk to service delivery and financial sustainability; lenders assessing creditworthiness need to understand capacity to manage borrowing alongside structural imbalance.
findings.figures: 2027/28: £25.7M (section 7.2); 3-year total £72,947k (Figure 1); current year gap exceeds £20M; preceding three years exceeded £30M each (section 4.4)
findings.quote: the Council facing a budget gap of £25.7M (before any increase in Council Tax) for the next financial year and follows on from the significant gaps in previous years

findings.paper_title: Report of the Deputy Chief Executive & Group Director of Corporate Resources
findings.headline: The council missed the statutory 31st May deadline for certifying draft accounts
findings.detail: Section 3.2 requires draft accounts to be certified by 31st May under the Accounts and Audit (Wales) Regulations. Section 3.3 confirms RCT certified draft accounts on 30th June 2026, one month late. Section 3.2 states that when deadlines are missed, councils must publish a statement setting out reasons for non-compliance; the paper confirms appropriate notices were published on the council website.
findings.matters: Missing statutory deadlines can indicate resource constraints or process issues in financial management, signalling potential governance weaknesses
findings.figures: 31st May statutory deadline; draft accounts certified 30th June 2026
findings.quote: If these timescales are not met then there is a requirement to publish a statement setting out the reasons for non-compliance. In accordance with these requirements, appropriate notices were published on the Council website.

findings.paper_title: Report of the Deputy Chief Executive & Group Director of Corporate Resources
findings.headline: General Fund Balances of £10.182M are at the Section 151 Officer's minimum acceptable level, with a plan to rebuild to £12.5M over three years
findings.detail: Section 6.3 establishes that the Section 151 Officer considers £10M the minimum General Fund Balance required for financial stability. At 31st March 2026, balances stand at £10.182M, leaving minimal headroom. The 2026/27 budget includes a £1M annual contribution to reserves over the medium-term planning period to rebuild to £12.5M.
findings.matters: General Fund Balances represent the council's financial buffer to handle unexpected pressures; at minimum acceptable level, the council has limited flexibility and the rebuilding plan depends on achieving annual surpluses
findings.figures: £10.182M at 31st March 2026; £10M minimum threshold; £12.5M planned minimum; £1M annual contribution
findings.quote: The Council's General Reserve balances at 31st March 2026 are £10.182M. The 2026/27 Revenue Budget Strategy includes budget provision for General Fund balances to be replenished via a £1M base budget for the period of the MTFP

findings.paper_title: Report of the Deputy Chief Executive & Group Director of Corporate Resources
findings.headline: The council required £1.175M of additional Welsh Government funding to manage in-year revenue pressures
findings.detail: Section 6.1 reports that the council needed £1.175M of additional (non-budgeted) Welsh Government funding to manage in-year pressures during 2025/26. Even with this supplementary funding, the council recorded a £0.058M net overspend. This indicates underlying revenue pressures of at least £1.2M that the council did not accommodate within its original budget.
findings.matters: Lenders need to assess whether a council can deliver its commitments from its own resources or whether it requires supplementary funding; reliance on additional government funding may indicate structural budget pressures
findings.figures: £1.175M additional Welsh Government funding required, £0.058M in-year overspend
findings.quote: the position against the revenue budget was a £0.058M in year overspend following the utilisation of additional Welsh Government funding of £1.175M to fund in year pressures.

findings.paper_title: Report of the Deputy Chief Executive & Group Director of Corporate Resources
findings.headline: Audit Wales will issue an unqualified auditor's report with no uncorrected material misstatements
findings.detail: The external audit has been completed with an unqualified opinion. Section 6.2 notes auditors identified a small number of misstatements which have been corrected. Section 8.1 confirms there are no uncorrected misstatements. This provides assurance that the council's financial statements are accurate and complete.
findings.matters: Lenders require assurance that the council's financial position is accurately reported and there are no hidden problems in the accounts
findings.figures: No uncorrected misstatements identified
findings.quote: Audit Wales intend to issue an unqualified auditor's report on the financial statements of Rhondda Cynon Taf County Borough Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Audit Enquiries Letter for RCT Management RCT CBC 2025-2026
findings.headline: Council faces forecasted medium-term budget gap with Welsh Government settlements unconfirmed
findings.detail: Welsh Government has not provided confirmation of future year financial settlements. The council is modeling scenarios and has forecasted a budget gap over the medium term requiring detailed service reviews to identify options to close it. General Reserve balances stand at £10.182M as at 31 March 2026; the council plans to replenish via £1M annual budget allocations through 2028/29, seeking to maintain a minimum level of £12.5M.
findings.matters: Lenders assess whether a council can balance its budget and has credible plans to close shortfalls. Unconfirmed government funding and a declared budget gap are material risks to financial sustainability.
findings.figures: General Reserve balances 31 March 2026: £10.182M; target minimum level: £12.5M; planned annual replenishment: £1M to financial year 2028/29
findings.quote: Welsh Government has not provided any confirmation of future year financial settlements, with the Council modelling potential scenarios via its MTFP.

findings.headline: The council holds £24.6m in non-treasury investments generating annual rental income of £2.0m.
findings.detail: Non-financial and commercial property investments comprise: Cynon Valley Waste Disposal Company (£2.985m), Ty Dysgu property (£2.980m with £0.324m annual rental), and other property holdings (£21.6m with £1.7m annual rental). These sit outside the core treasury position.
findings.matters: These investments expose the council to property market risk and income volatility outside mainstream treasury operations. Material values are subject to revaluation and rental income dependency.
findings.figures: Cynon Valley Waste: £2.985m. Ty Dysgu: £2.980m (annual rental £0.324m). Other properties: £21.6m (annual rental £1.7m). Total non-treasury investments: approximately £27.565m.
findings.quote: These buildings have a fair value of £21.6M, with an annual rental of £1.7M.

findings.headline: Investment returns of 3.83% underperformed the benchmark of 4.05% by 22 basis points.
findings.detail: The council's cash balances of £86.2m on average earned 3.83% during 2025/26, slightly below the 7-day money market benchmark of 4.05%. The council maintained a low-risk investment strategy in line with its Treasury Management Strategy.
findings.matters: Shows the trade-off between risk minimisation and investment returns. The minor underperformance suggests either conservative cash positioning or reduced yields on compliant low-risk instruments.
findings.figures: Interest Received: £3.340m. Average Cash Balance: £86.206m. Return on Investments: 3.83%. Benchmark Return: 4.05%. Interest foregone: approximately £0.017m (22bp × £86.206m average balance).
findings.quote: The average return on investments has slightly under-performed the benchmark return over the year.

findings.headline: The council has committed to £56.1m new borrowing for the Sustainable Communities for Learning (schools) programme.
findings.detail: For Tranche 1 of a new rolling schools investment programme, the council's contribution is £84.8m (£28.7m from existing funds and £56.1m new borrowing). This represents 20% of total investment. Revenue implications are phased from 2029/30 onwards.
findings.matters: A material future borrowing commitment that will increase debt service costs from 2029/30, affecting medium-term affordability. The scale and timing of revenue impact needs monitoring.
findings.figures: Council contribution: £84.8m. Borrowing element: £56.1m. Borrowing as % of total investment: 20%. Total Tranche 1 investment: £280.8m.
findings.quote: The latest modelled Council contribution level is £84.8M comprising £28.7M of existing funds and £56.1M of borrowing, as approved by Council on 4th March 2026.

findings.headline: Financing costs as a proportion of revenue were 4.87%, better than the 4.99% forecast.
findings.detail: The ratio of capital financing costs to net revenue stream came in at 4.87% against the budgeted 4.99%, a 12 basis point improvement. This reflects better interest rate management and lower average debt levels than anticipated.
findings.matters: Shows the council's capacity to service debt relative to revenue is stronger than budgeted, improving headroom for other commitments.
findings.figures: Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream 2025/26: Original Estimate 4.99%, Actual 4.87%.
findings.quote: Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream 4.99% [Original Estimate] 4.87% [Actual]

findings.headline: Capital expenditure came in at £138.4m against a budget of £166.0m—an underspend of £27.6m.
findings.detail: The council's capital programme delivered £138.411m of the planned £166.036m in 2025/26, a variance of 16.6%. This suggests either slower project delivery or better project management than forecast.
findings.matters: Shows the council's ability or inability to execute planned investment at the pace projected, which shapes borrowing needs and interest cost.
findings.figures: 2025/26 Original Capital Expenditure estimate: £166.036m. 2025/26 Actual: £138.411m.
findings.quote: Capital Expenditure 166.036 [Original Estimate] 138.411 [Actual]

findings.headline: Gross debt was £76.2m lower than forecast, at £327.6m against budget of £403.8m.
findings.detail: Actual gross debt of £327.630m (31 March 2026) significantly undershot the original estimate of £403.755m. The variance of £76.125m suggests either lower capital delivery than anticipated or better-than-planned cash generation.
findings.matters: A material variance in debt position suggests either capital programme delivery is slower than planned, or cash management is stronger—both material to assessing financial stability.
findings.figures: Gross Debt 2025/26 Original Estimate: £403.755m. Gross Debt 2025/26 Actual: £327.630m. Variance: £76.125m lower.
findings.quote: Gross Debt * 403.755 [Original Estimate] 327.630 [Actual 31st March 2026]

findings.headline: Total debt fell by £12.4m during 2025/26 through repayment of short-term borrowing.
findings.detail: The council reduced borrowing from £285.004m to £272.585m, with short-term loans of £15m and £5m repaid. Average debt interest rate was 3.97%. The council's policy of maximising internal borrowing and running down cash balances continued.
findings.matters: Demonstrates active debt management and reducing reliance on external funding, improving the council's financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Total debt movement: -£12.419m. Opening balance £285.004m, closing £272.585m. Loans repaid: £15m and £5m.
findings.quote: Short term borrowing was taken during 2025/26 for cashflow purposes and loans of £15M and £5M were repaid during 2025/26.

findings.headline: No material uncertainties identified regarding the council's ability to continue as a going concern.
findings.detail: Based on audit procedures, the Auditor General has identified no material uncertainties relating to events or conditions that could cast doubt on the council's ability to continue as a going concern for at least 12 months from financial statement authorisation.
findings.matters: Going concern clearance is fundamental for lenders; it provides assurance the council can meet its financial obligations in the foreseeable future.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: I have not identified any material uncertainties relating to events or conditions that, individually or collectively, may cast significant doubt on Rhondda Cynon Taf County Borough Council and its Group's ability to continue to adopt the going concern basis of accounting for a period of at least twelve months

findings.headline: Auditors identified a material population of fully depreciated vehicles remaining on the asset register despite disposal.
findings.detail: Testing found £1.4m of gross assets at nil book value that no longer belonged to the council. The audit risk assessment noted that a material population of fully depreciated vehicles remain recorded in the register, indicating the council's vehicle disposal and asset register review processes are not operating effectively.
findings.matters: Asset register management failures suggest potential weaknesses in the control environment and accountability for council assets, relevant to assessing overall financial governance quality.
findings.quote: There is a risk of material misstatement due to a material population of fully depreciated vehicles remaining on the asset register.

findings.headline: Auditors identified and corrected material misstatements totalling approximately £10.5 million before finalising accounts.
findings.detail: Corrections included £4.4m debtor/creditor misclassification on grant accounting, £3.5m asset classification error for construction project, £1.4m fully depreciated assets no longer belonging to council, £1m overstatement of capital commitments, and £0.8m cash flow calculation error. All misstatements were corrected by management before finalisation, with no material uncorrected misstatements remaining.
findings.matters: The volume and nature of corrections—spanning grant processing, asset register, capital commitments, and cash flow—suggest control weaknesses in the accounts close-down process that could affect future financial reporting reliability.
findings.figures: £4,410k (debtors/creditors), £3,548k (PPE classification), £1,358k (disposed assets), £979k (capital commitments), £774k (cash flow statement)
findings.quote: During our audit, we identified misstatements that have been corrected by management, but which we consider should be drawn to your attention.

findings.headline: Council has received an unqualified audit opinion on 2025-26 accounts and will have them certified ahead of the 30 September deadline.
findings.detail: The Auditor General intends to issue an unqualified opinion on both the council and group accounts. Auditors plan to certify the accounts on 24 September 2026, six days before the statutory deadline. The council produced a high-quality set of accounts and continued to work effectively with auditors throughout the process.
findings.matters: Unqualified opinions and early completion are key signals of financial reliability and control quality for lenders evaluating creditworthiness and financial management capability.
findings.figures: Certification date 24 September 2026; statutory deadline 30 September 2026
findings.quote: We intend to issue an unqualified opinion on the accounts. We are aiming to certify your accounts on 24 September 2026, which is ahead of the deadline of 30 September 2026.

findings.headline: The council is committed to a £191m three-year capital programme while capital financing charges of £21.5-£23m annually are embedded in a revenue budget under severe pressure.
findings.detail: Section 14.3 sets out a three-year capital programme of £191m with £19.4m additional investment (including £14.1m from earmarked reserves, £2.2m reallocated funding, and £3.0m LGBI borrowing). Section 7.2 shows capital financing charges rising from £21.5m (2026/27) to £23.0m (2029/30). Capital obligations are non-discretionary and must be funded alongside the £73m revenue gap.
findings.matters: Non-discretionary capital financing charges compete with service spending in a revenue budget facing a £73m structural deficit. Debt service obligations limit the council's ability to respond flexibly to emerging pressures or invest in transformation.
findings.figures: £191m three-year capital programme; £19.380m additional investment; capital financing charges £21.519m (2026/27) to £23.019m (2029/30)
findings.quote: The three-year programme amounts to £ 191M and includes further additional available funding of £19.380M for investment in priorities aligned to the Council's Corporate Plan

findings.headline: Secondary school reserves have moved into deficit (£805k) in 2025/26 despite the Individual Schools Budget receiving above-inflation funding increases.
findings.detail: Table 5.2 shows secondary school reserves fell from £290k surplus (March 2025) to £805k deficit (March 2026), a £1.1m adverse movement in one year. Total school reserves across all sectors declined from £5.8m to £5.3m. This occurs despite the ISB growing 48% over the past decade versus 37% for other council services, receiving an extra £15.5m above the council's growth rate.
findings.matters: Schools are a core service; deficits signal either unmanaged cost pressures or insufficient funding despite preferential treatment. Ongoing deficit spending is not sustainable and may lead to service cuts or require council bailout from an already-stretched revenue budget.
findings.figures: Secondary schools: £290k surplus → £805k deficit in 2025/26; Total ISB reserves £5.8m → £5.3m; ISB grew 48% in 10 years vs council 37%
findings.quote: The 2025/26 year-end position has decreased compared to the previous year, as schools responsibly utilised reserves to supplement their budgets and provide a wide range of provision to support learners.

findings.headline: General reserves of £10.2m are maintained at their statutory minimum despite the revenue budget having more than doubled since 2003, constraining financial flexibility.
findings.detail: The council has maintained minimum general reserves of £10m continuously since 2003/04 when the annual budget was £320m; the budget now stands at £710m, meaning reserves have fallen from 3% to 1.4% of annual spending. Recent usage for Storm Bert response (November 2024) means reserves are at their floor. The council's finance director plans to raise this minimum to £12.5m by end-2028/29, requiring £1m annual contributions.
findings.matters: Thin reserves reduce a council's ability to absorb service demand shocks, invest in transformation, or maintain service continuity during budget pressures. At 1.4% of budget, RCT has minimal buffer. The council could not use reserves to bridge its gap—doing so would require £150m of reserves, leaving a still-unresolved £73m base budget cut.
findings.figures: £10.182m reserves at 31 March 2026; minimum £10m maintained since 2003/04 (when budget was £320m); target minimum £12.5m by end-2028/29
findings.quote: The level of General Fund Reserves (i.e. the Council's working balance) have been maintained at a minimum level of £10M since financial year 2003/04, when the annual revenue budget was set at £320M.

findings.headline: Welsh Government has not confirmed future funding settlements, leaving the council unable to plan with certainty despite 78% funding dependency on WG.
findings.detail: Section 3.2 states that to date, WG has provided no indication of future settlements. With WG funding accounting for 78% of RCT's revenue budget, each 1% change in settlement equates to £5.6m variance for this council. The budget gap could range from £55.4m (if WG grows at 3% p.a.) to £90.1m (at 1% growth), a £35m swing driven by unknowable WG decisions.
findings.matters: A lender requires visibility of revenue stability and funding certainty. A £35m range of possible deficits—dependent on external decisions not yet announced—materially increases planning risk and could force late-year service cuts or borrowing decisions.
findings.figures: 78% of revenue budget from WG; £5.6m per 1% change in settlement; £55.4m gap (at +3% WG growth) vs £90.1m (at +1%)
findings.quote: To date, Welsh Government has not provided an indication of future year financial settlements, with local authorities modelling potential scenarios themselves

findings.headline: The council faces a cumulative budget gap of £72.9m over three years (base case), described as the most significant budget challenge it has ever faced.
findings.detail: Table 10.1 projects deficits of £25.7m (2027/28), £25.6m (2028/29) and £21.7m (2029/30) even with 3% council tax increases and assuming 2% annual Welsh Government funding growth. The council must balance its budget by 11 March 2027 under a statutory duty. The paper notes this follows deficits of £38m, £36m, £36m and £22m in 2023/24-2026/27.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can afford its current spending commitments and maintain essential service delivery without using reserves or raising additional borrowing.
findings.quote: the most significant budget gaps it has ever faced of £38M, £36M, £36M and £22M in 2023/24 2024/25, 2025/26 and 2026/27 respectively as well as year-on-year budget gaps in other years over the last decade.

findings.headline: Welsh Government grants for coal tip remediation and flood management continue into 2026/27
findings.detail: The council continues to receive capital and revenue grants from Welsh Government for coal tips work and flood management. Specific projects mentioned include Phase 4 of Llanwonno Tip at Tylorstown and Graig du Dinas Tip. This external funding enables significant remediation and resilience work.
findings.matters: External funding reduces the council's own spending obligation; loss of this funding stream would require the council to fund these assets from its own resources.
findings.figures: Amount not quantified
findings.quote: Welsh Government Coal Tips related capital and revenue grants continue into 2026/27 with major works continuing on Phase 4 of Llanwonno Tip at Tylorstown, and Graig du Dinas Tip.

findings.headline: The highways network is valued at £3.4 billion and has received 14 years of enhanced investment levels
findings.detail: The council's highways network is described as 'the most significant asset of the Council' comprising carriageways, footways, bridges, retaining walls, culverts, street lighting, traffic signals and safety barriers. The council has maintained enhanced investment levels for fourteen years and plans to continue through 2026/27.
findings.matters: This is material to the council's balance sheet and asset base; sustained investment levels in the largest council asset indicate either legacy maintenance deficit or strategic prioritization of this area.
findings.figures: £3.4Bn valuation; 14 years of enhanced investment
findings.quote: The Highways Network represents the most significant asset of the Council, valued in at over £3.4Bn and comprises of carriageways, footways, structures (bridges, retaining walls, culverts, etc.), street lighting, traffic signals and signs, safety barriers, highway drainage, etc.

findings.headline: Cabinet has delegated authority to suspend projects and reallocate capital funding at the Director's discretion
findings.detail: The Director of Environmental Services is authorised to 'suspend programmes/projects and reallocate funding to optimise delivery' during the year, subject to consultation. The report justifies this by noting 'it is vital to maintain the flexibility to review projects on a case-by-case basis around deliverability and risk.'
findings.matters: The need for this delegated flexibility indicates the council does not expect to deliver the capital programme as originally scoped; it shows execution risk and a strategy to preserve cash by allowing project suspension.
findings.figures: £9.900M (total fungible allocation)
findings.quote: delegate authority to the Director of Environmental Services to extend activity to deliver additional projects during the financial year, where capacity exists for accelerated delivery in accordance with the purpose of the wider programme, or to suspend programmes/projects and reallocate funding to optimise delivery.

findings.headline: Storm Bert has created an additional fully-funded emergency infrastructure repair programme alongside the capital programme
findings.detail: The council is delivering a significant additional programme of work to repair infrastructure destroyed by Storm Bert, described as 'fully funded'. This includes bridges, roads, culverts, retaining walls and landslide repairs. The council notes 'the frequent and unprecedented floods in recent years continue to represent a significant body of work' and ongoing legacy issues related to former coal tips.
findings.matters: Emergency repair obligations create both funding opportunity (if external funding is secured) and financial stress (if it competes with planned spending); it signals climate and flooding risk exposure of the council's asset base.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: The Council's ambitious capital programme continues to be delivered alongside the significant additional and fully funded programme of work attributable to the destruction to infrastructure caused by Storm Bert.

findings.headline: Supply chain shortages, high inflation and resource constraints are ongoing pressures on programme delivery
findings.detail: The council identifies persistent external factors affecting delivery: volatility in construction costs, availability of skills and resources, and competition for road space from other utilities. The report warns that 'Programme delivery and coordination will remain immensely challenging due to supply chain challenges and cost escalation.'
findings.matters: These are material risks to the council's ability to deliver the capital programme on budget and on time, affecting the council's project execution capability.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: In recent years, the programme has been impacted by a number of external factors, including supply chain shortages, high inflation and internal resource constraints. These factors continue to persist, particularly and not exclusive to volatility in construction costs, availability of skills and resources

findings.headline: Capital programme is subject to formal approval not yet given
findings.detail: The £9.900M allocation for Highways and Engineering Services is conditional on Cabinet and Council approving the Corporate Plan Investment Priorities Report on 23 September 2026. The report notes explicitly that this allocation is contingent on that approval; without it, the funding is not committed.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know which capital commitments are firm and which remain conditional; this cannot be treated as committed spend until approved.
findings.quote: Subject to the approval by Cabinet of the "Council Corporate Plan – Investment Priorities Report" and Council on 23rd September 2026., this report sets out the supplementary capital programme for Highways and Engineering Services.

findings.headline: School funding increases are modelled to exceed both Welsh Government settlement levels and the funding available to non-school services.
findings.detail: Section 7.8 commits to continuing preferential school funding. The MTFP "would see school funding levels increasing far in excess of the modelled Welsh Government settlement levels and in excess of the resources allocated to non-school services." Schools receive uplifts of £10.8M (2027/28), £7.9M (2028/29), and £7.9M (2029/30) within the additional budget requirement.
findings.matters: Schools ring-fencing comes at direct expense of other services (social care, waste, highways). A lender must assess whether non-school services are approaching service failure and whether school budgets are realistic or will face cuts next cycle.
findings.quote: The modelling assumptions within the updated MTFP continues this approach and would see school funding levels increasing far in excess of the modelled Welsh Government settlement levels and in excess of the resources allocated to non-school services.

findings.headline: Council tax is modelled to increase at 3% per annum across the planning period, contributing £4.5M to £4.7M annually to close the gap.
findings.detail: Section 5.3 sets council tax increases at "3.00% per annum" for all three years. The base case assumes council tax generates approximately £4.5M in 2027/28, £4.6M in 2028/29, and £4.7M in 2029/30 towards closing the budget gap.
findings.matters: Council tax is within the council's control and 3% is near levels at which taxpayer objection typically increases. A lender wants to understand available headroom and risk of hitting political or referendum resistance.
findings.quote: Council Tax increases are currently being modelled at 3.00% per annum.

findings.headline: The council advises that revisions to service delivery arrangements and staffing levels are "highly likely" as a result of continued significant budget gaps.
findings.detail: Section 7.4 states that while services and jobs will be safeguarded "wherever possible", it is "highly likely that revisions to some service delivery arrangements will be required and associated staffing levels". The council has committed to identifying further savings options across all services and notes that "as a last resort", it will propose reductions in service levels.
findings.matters: Service reductions and redundancies indicate the council cannot manage financial pressure within current operating scope. A lender will want to track which services are at risk, whether consultation occurs, and whether cuts generate second-order demand (welfare, social stability).
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: it is highly likely that revisions to some service delivery arrangements will be required and associated staffing levels, based on the continued significant budget gaps which we face

findings.headline: Every 1% change in Welsh Government resource settlement creates a £5.6M swing in the council's budget gap across the planning period.
findings.detail: The council models three settlement scenarios: 1%, 2%, and 3% annual increases. At 3%, the three-year gap is £55.4M; at 2%, it is £72.9M; at 1%, it reaches £90.1M. A single percentage point difference in Welsh Government's funding decision produces a £34.7M variance in cumulative budget pressure, illustrating structural dependence on decisions outside the council's control.
findings.matters: The council's financial stability depends on Welsh Government funding decisions beyond its control. A lender must understand this dependency and whether the council has contingency plans if settlement is worse than assumed.
findings.figures: £5.6M per 1% change; £55.409M gap at 3% growth, £72.947M at 2%, £90.144M at 1%
findings.quote: the budget gap at £5.6M per 1%

findings.headline: Using reserves alone to balance the budget would require over £150M, yet the council would still face a £73M permanent base budget reduction by the end of the planning period.
findings.detail: Section 8.3 explains that to cover the full three-year budget gap through reserves would require over £150M, yet this would still leave a £73M structural deficit requiring permanent service cuts. This signals that permanent reductions in expenditure or service scope, not reserve drawdowns, must be the main mechanism.
findings.matters: Reserves are finite and non-renewable. A lender needs assurance that the council is making permanent structural adjustments to expenditure rather than relying on one-off funding. Reserve depletion at this rate signals unsustainable service delivery.
findings.figures: £150M of reserves required; £73M permanent base budget reduction still needed at end of period
findings.quote: to balance the budget (base case), using reserves alone would require the use of over £150M of reserves and the Council would still have a need to reduce its base budget by approximately £73M at the end of this period

findings.headline: The council faces a cumulative three-year budget gap of £59.2M (2027/28 to 2029/30) under base case modelling, following gaps of £20M+ and £30M+ in prior years.
findings.detail: Under the base case assumption of 2% Welsh Government settlement increases, the council must find savings of £25.7M in 2027/28, £21.0M in 2028/29, and £16.9M in 2029/30. This represents persistence of annual deficits: the current year faces a gap of £20M+, and the three years before that each exceeded £30M.
findings.matters: A lender must understand whether the council has a credible plan to close a gap of this magnitude without exhausting reserves or failing its statutory duty to set a balanced budget by 11 March 2027.
findings.figures: £25,724k (2027/28), £20,958k (2028/29), £16,941k (2029/30), cumulative £59,164k; prior year gap £20M+; preceding three years £30M+ each
findings.quote: Base Case Remaining Gap 21,264 20,958 16,941 59,164

findings.headline: Council tax increase effectiveness eroded: 19.5% of any rise lost to Council Tax Reduction Scheme costs
findings.detail: Proposed 4% council tax increase generates £1.429M additional income per 1% increase but costs £0.278M in additional Council Tax Reduction Scheme (CTRS) support, netting only £1.151M per 1% increase. This means nearly 1 in 5 council tax revenue is diverted to subsidizing bills for lower-income households. The paper notes 42% of RCT properties are in Band A (lowest band).
findings.matters: The council's ability to raise revenue through council tax is severely constrained by welfare support costs it must fund. This income source is less reliable and lower-yielding than assumed by councils elsewhere.
findings.figures: 1% Council Tax increase gross: £1.429M; CTRS cost: £0.278M; net: £1.151M; leakage: 19.5%; Band A properties: 42% of RCT housing stock
findings.quote: A 1% increase in Council Tax will generate an additional income for the Council of £1.429M (at the 2026/27 tax base level) but will also cost £0.278M in additional CTRS requirements. It therefore follows that a 1% increase generates a net additional income of £1.151M, or stated another way, 19.5% of any Council Tax increase is lost to support the increased costs associated with Welsh Government's CTRS.

findings.headline: School reserves depleted from £20M to £6M in four years, requiring continued council subsidy
findings.detail: School aggregate balances collapsed from £20M (March 2022) to £6M (March 2025), a 70% drawdown. Schools received significant one-off Welsh Government resources and were 'previously advised to use their reserves responsibly.' The council is now allocating full inflationary funding plus £1M for ALN/special school capacity (5.6% cash increase in ISB). Schools budget increased 45% over 10 years vs 32% for other services, representing £18.6M extra allocation.
findings.matters: School reserves cannot buffer future cost pressures. The council is now committed to protecting school budgets, which limits flexibility elsewhere and signals structural cost pressures in demand-led services.
findings.figures: School balances: £20M (2021/22) → £6M (31 March 2025); ISB increase 2026/27: £12.005M (5.6%); ALN enhancement: £1M; 10-year ISB increase 45% vs other services 32% (£18.6M differential)
findings.quote: For context, the aggregate level of school balances increased from £2M to £20M over the course of the financial years 2020/21 and 2021/22 and have now reduced to £6M at the 31st March 2025.

findings.headline: Single-year settlement with no forward visibility creates medium-term budget planning uncertainty
findings.detail: Welsh Government provided only a single-year settlement for 2026/27 with no indication of future year funding levels. The final settlement improved to 4.5% only after a budget agreement that included £112.8M nationally for local government. The council notes 'The settlement provides no indication of future year settlement levels.' This follows a pattern of provisional, then final settlements, making MTFP forecasting speculative.
findings.matters: Without forward visibility, councils cannot plan debt repayment, capital programmes, or service restructuring with confidence. Single-year certainty forces repeated emergency budget cycles.
findings.figures: 2026/27 settlement increase: 2.7% provisional (24 Nov 2025), improved to 4.5% final (20 Jan 2026 after £112.8M national top-up); settlement range across Wales 4.1% to 6.1%
findings.quote: The settlement provides no indication of future year settlement levels.

findings.headline: Efficiency savings approaching exhaustion point with increasing impact on frontline services
findings.detail: The council has delivered £40M+ in efficiency and service reconfiguration measures over three years. Senior leadership now explicitly states that 'following the delivery of over £40M of efficiency measures over the last 3 years... it is becoming increasingly difficult to deliver such opportunities without impacting on front line services.' The 2026/27 efficiency target of £6.335M is identified as increasingly challenging to achieve.
findings.matters: Once a council exhausts efficiency savings, the only levers left are service cuts, borrowing, or further tax rises. This signals a tightening financial straitjacket for future years.
findings.figures: £40M+ efficiency measures over 3 years; £6.335M target for 2026/27 (from: General Efficiencies £3.031M, Non-Pay Freeze £0.976M, Restructuring £1.265M, External Funding £1.063M)
findings.quote: following the delivery of over £40M of efficiency measures over the last 3 years, as part of us balancing the largest budget gaps we have ever experienced as a Council, it is becoming increasingly difficult to deliver such opportunities without impacting on front line services.

findings.headline: Three consecutive years of unprecedented budget gaps now forcing reliance on transitional reserves
findings.detail: The council faced £36M budget gaps annually for the last three years. For 2026/27, after efficiency measures and council tax increases, they still need £0.911M from reserves to balance, reducing their transitional reserve from £4.745M to £3.834M. The deputy Chief Executive notes this 'does not deal with the underlying recurring budget issue into the future.'
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can sustain service delivery and debt repayment when it requires reserve drawdowns every year and savings are becoming harder to find without affecting frontline services.
findings.figures: £36M annual gap × 3 years; £6.335M efficiencies delivered 2026/27; £0.911M reserve drawdown; £40M+ total efficiencies over 3 years
findings.quote: Over the last 3 financial years our budget strategies have had to address the largest budget gaps this Council has ever faced at around £36M for each year.

findings.paper_title: 4. Central South Consortium Joint Education Service Joint Committee Detailed Audit Plan 2025
findings.headline: Audit fee increased 15% — significantly above the 1.7% national average — due to cessation complexity and funding changes.
findings.detail: The audit fee for 2024-25 is £25,502 and represents a 15% increase, far exceeding the national average 1.7% increase published by Audit Wales. This exceptional increase is explicitly attributed to complexity arising from the Joint Committee's cessation and a reduction in materiality due to changes in funding arrangements.
findings.matters: A 15% audit fee increase signals material financial complexity and governance risk beyond routine auditing; the explicit link to cessation and funding changes indicates significant transition financial work ahead.
findings.figures: 15% increase; £25,502 estimated fee; national average 1.7%
findings.quote: Due to the additional complexity arising from the cessation of the Joint Committee and the impact of a reduction in materiality due to changes in funding arrangements, the fee rate increase for this year has been agreed at 15%.

findings.paper_title: 4. Central South Consortium Joint Education Service Joint Committee Detailed Audit Plan 2025
findings.headline: The Joint Committee will cease in its current form on 31st August 2025, with services transferred elsewhere.
findings.detail: The Central South Consortium Joint Education Service is ending and services will transfer to a new regional service or to Local Authorities. This creates potential impact on accounts production and audit process, and requires consideration of a 5-month set of accounts for 2025-26. The host council is Rhondda Cynon Taff.
findings.matters: Cessation of a joint service creates uncertainty about asset and liability transfers, affects the host council's financial position, and signals structural change in education service delivery.
findings.figures: 31st August 2025
findings.quote: The Joint Committee is due to end in its current form on 31st August 2025, with services being transferred to a new regional service or to Local Authorities.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1-Statement of Accounts RCT Pension Fund
findings.headline: Wales Pension Partnership restructuring to establish independent Investment Management Company
findings.detail: RCT's pension fund is part of WPP, an 8-fund pool covering all Welsh councils. The UK Government mandated LGPS restructuring through the 'Fit for the Future' consultation. WPP decided to establish its own IMCo rather than merge with another pool. Government approved the business case on 9 April 2025; RCT Council approved this on 25 June 2025; implementation deadline is March 2026.
findings.matters: Structural changes to pension fund investment management affect fee structures, investment strategy, and long-term returns, all material to the council's pension liability position and relevant to lenders assessing council financial resilience
findings.figures: WPP manages £4.8bn in assets for 8 Welsh LGPS funds covering 22 local authorities, 382 employers, and 412,000 scheme members
findings.quote: The formation of WPP IMCo presents an opportunity to create a stand-alone LGPS Investment Company for the benefit of all the stakeholders of the underlying 22 local authorities in Wales, 382 employers and 412,000 members.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Audit Enquiries Letter Management RCT CBC 2024-25
findings.headline: Continued reliance on unregistered children's homes due to shortage of registered capacity
findings.detail: The council faces ongoing risk of having to place looked-after children in settings recorded as Operating Without Registration (OWR) by the Care Inspectorate for Wales, due to scarcity of registered home supply. This creates regulatory, safeguarding and financial exposure. The council is working to reduce OWR reliance through its Looked After Children strategy, supported by Welsh Government grant funding, but the challenge remains flagged as high priority.
findings.matters: Reliance on unregistered placements represents regulatory risk, potential reputational damage, and may indicate cost pressures or gaps in provision that could require unplanned expenditure. This is material to understanding the council's service delivery risks.
findings.figures: No specific numbers provided; issue flagged in Strategic Risk Register
findings.quote: Challenges remain around the sufficiency of registered children's homes with the continued risk of the Council being unable to avoid reliance upon settings that are recorded as Operating Without Registration (OWR) by the Care Inspectorate for Wales (CIW).

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Audit Enquiries Letter Management RCT CBC 2024-25
findings.headline: General Fund reserves below minimum threshold following Storm Bert drawdown
findings.detail: Reserves fell to £9.240M following £1M drawdown in November 2024 to support Storm Bert recovery. The Section 151 Officer views a minimum of £10M as essential for financial flexibility and stability. The council plans to replenish reserves in 2025/26, but near-term shortfall reduces buffer against unforeseen pressures.
findings.matters: Underfunded reserves constrain financial resilience and limit the council's ability to respond to emergencies or absorb overspends, which is particularly concerning given the identified budget gap.
findings.figures: Reserves £9.240M vs minimum target £10M; £1M drawn for Storm Bert in November 2024
findings.quote: The Council's General Reserve balances at 31st March 2025 were £9.240M (draft, subject to audit), further to the utilisation of £1M in 2024/25 to support local residents and businesses in their recovery and targeted resilience following Storm Bert in November 2024.

findings.paper_title: Report of the Group Director of Finance, Digital & Frontline Services
findings.headline: General Fund Balances fell to £9.240M, below the Section 151 Officer's stated minimum of £10M
findings.detail: The council's General Fund Balances at 31st March 2025 are £9.240M, down from £10.240M a year earlier. This falls short of the minimum level identified by the Section 151 Officer as necessary for 'financial flexibility and stability going forward'. The £1M year-on-year decrease was driven by a draw for Storm Bert recovery (November 2024) plus use of additional Welsh Government funding to meet in-year revenue pressures.
findings.matters: Reserves operating below the authority's own policy minimum indicate reduced financial headroom and flexibility. Coupled with in-year reserve draws to cover specific events, this signals tightening financial position and potential constraints on discretionary activity.
findings.figures: General Fund Balances £9.240M (policy minimum £10M); £1M Storm Bert recovery draw; £1.917M additional Welsh Government funding used to balance budget
findings.quote: it is my view, as Section 151 Officer, that £10M represents the minimum level of General Fund Balances the Council should maintain to ensure financial flexibility and stability going forward.

news_drafts.headline: Rhondda Cynon Taff gets clean audit but must fix vehicle disposal records
news_drafts.lead: Rhondda Cynon Taff Council has received an unqualified audit opinion on its 2025–26 accounts and will have them certified on 24 September, six days ahead of the statutory deadline. The Auditor General found the council produced "a high-quality set of accounts" and identified no material uncertainties about its ability to continue as a going concern. However, auditors identified a material control weakness: £1.4m of fully depreciated vehicles remain recorded on the asset register despite having been disposed of. The audit report states that "a material population of fully depreciated vehicles remain recorded in the register," indicating the council's vehicle disposal and asset register review processes are "not operating effectively." The council corrected all material misstatements totalling £10.5m before finalisation.

news_drafts.headline: Rhondda Cynon Taff council warns service cuts are 'highly likely' as £59m shortfall looms
news_drafts.lead: Rhondda Cynon Taff council must find £59.2m over three years from 2027/28 to 2029/30 to balance its budget, the cabinet heard on 21 September. The council warned that revisions to service delivery arrangements and associated staffing levels are "highly likely" as a result. This follows three consecutive years of deficits each exceeding £30m and a current-year shortfall of more than £20m. The council's analysis shows that even using reserves — money a council has set aside — to cover the shortfall would require over £150m, and would still leave a £73m permanent reduction in its base budget, signalling that permanent service cuts rather than temporary borrowing must be the main mechanism for addressing the problem.

news_drafts.headline: Rhondda Cynon Taff warns of service cuts as three-year budget gap reaches £59.2m
news_drafts.lead: Rhondda Cynon Taff Council faces a cumulative budget gap — the difference between planned spending and expected income — of £59.2 million across the next three years, following annual shortfalls above £20 million in the current year and above £30 million in each of the three years before. The council has warned that service delivery changes and staffing cuts are "highly likely". Even using £150 million in reserves, money the council has put aside, would not close the gap; the council would still need permanent spending cuts of £73 million by the end of the planning period. The deficit is highly sensitive to funding from Welsh Government: a one percentage point change in annual funding creates a £5.6 million swing in budget pressure across the three years. The council is modelling council tax increases of 3 per cent a year to contribute £4.5 million to £4.7 million towards closing the gap.
